title: Orbitz showed Mac users pricier hotels first
hook: Same room, same price, but a different order of results depending on your computer.
collected: The visitor's operating system (Mac or PC), which every website can read.
inferred: Mac users tended to spend more: Orbitz's data suggested $20-30 more per night on average.
done: Orbitz tested ranking pricier hotels higher for Mac users. This was steering (changing the order), not charging Mac users more for the same room.
affected: Mac users searching for hotels on Orbitz.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Reported by the Wall Street Journal and confirmed by Orbitz as a test (company admission).

companyResponse.text: Orbitz said the same room cost the same on any computer, and users could sort results by price.

sources.title: On Orbitz, Mac Users Steered to Pricier Hotels
Orbitz profiles Mac users with pricier hotels

limits: Paywalled original. Often misreported as 'Mac users charged 30% more', which is not what happened.
whyItMatters: Reordering what you see can change what you pay without any price changing.

title: Staples online prices varied by distance to rival stores
hook: The price online depended on whether a competitor's store was near you.
collected: Approximate location from the visitor's IP address.
howObtained: Every website sees your IP address.
inferred: Whether an OfficeMax or Office Depot store was nearby (roughly within 20 miles).
done: The Wall Street Journal tested prices from tens of thousands of ZIP codes and found higher online prices where rival stores were far away. In practice, lower-income areas were less likely to see the lower price.
affected: Online shoppers in areas without nearby competitors.
label: REPORTED
labelNote: Investigative journalism with a described test method.

companyResponse.text: Staples said prices vary based on factors such as local costs.

sources.title: Websites Vary Prices, Deals Based on Users' Information
Staples online prices change based on location

limits: Original paywalled; detailed figures come from secondary coverage.
whyItMatters: A neutral-sounding signal (distance) can still produce unequal outcomes.

title: Princeton Review tutoring prices by ZIP code
hook: Areas with many Asian residents were 1.8 times as likely to be quoted a higher price.
collected: The ZIP code a customer typed in.
howObtained: Required to see a price for online SAT tutoring.
inferred: Which regional price tier to show.
done: ProPublica found Premier SAT tutoring priced from $6,600 to $8,400 by ZIP code. Customers in areas with a high share of Asian residents were 1.8 times as likely to be offered higher prices, regardless of income.
label: REPORTED
labelNote: Investigative data analysis. The company confirmed regional pricing but disputes that it is discrimination.

companyResponse.text: The Princeton Review said prices reflect regional costs and competition, and that calling this discrimination "misconstrues both the literal, legal and moral meaning of the word".

sources.title: Asians Nearly Twice as Likely to Get Higher Price from Princeton Review

limits: Correlation at ZIP-code level. Does not show the company intended a racial effect. Correlation is not intent.
whyItMatters: Even crude geographic pricing can line up with race.

title: Measuring price discrimination and steering on 16 sites
hook: Researchers used real users and fake accounts to catch personalised prices in the act.
collected: Account status, browsing history, device type (mobile vs desktop).
inferred: Which prices or result orders to show.
done: Hannak et al. (ACM IMC 2014) tested 10 retailers and 6 travel sites with about 300 real users plus control accounts. They found personalisation on 9 of 16: price differences on Cheaptickets and Orbitz (logged-in members), steering on Expedia and Hotels.com, and mobile differences on Home Depot and Travelocity.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Peer-reviewed measurement. Most individual experiments found no personalisation; the 9 of 16 refers to sites with at least some evidence.

sources.title: Is the price right? Study finds price discrimination online
Measuring Price Discrimination and Steering on E-commerce Web Sites

limits: 2014 data; sites change their systems constantly.
whyItMatters: This is how you test for personalisation properly: controlled accounts, at the same time, changing one thing. Try it in the Auditor's Lab.

title: FTC study: the tools for 'surveillance pricing' exist
hook: Companies sell software that can use mouse movements and abandoned carts to set prices.
collected: Location, demographics, browsing history, mouse movements, items left in a cart, according to documents from pricing intermediaries.
howObtained: Retailers' own data plus third-party data, processed by pricing vendors.
inferred: Willingness to pay and the 'right' price or offer for an individual.
done: FTC staff reviewed documents from 6 intermediaries (Mastercard, Accenture, PROS, Bloomreach, Revionics and McKinsey) serving at least 250 clients, and found their products can use such data to set individualised prices or offers.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Regulator study. It documents CAPABILITY, not actual use: the report used only hypothetical examples. Capability is not proof of use.

outcome.text: Preliminary findings released on a 3-2 vote; the two Republican commissioners dissented. The new chair later closed the public comment request. Later status is unclear.

sources.title: FTC Surveillance Pricing Study Indicates Wide Range of Personal Data Used to Set Individualized Consumer Prices

limits: No named retailer was shown using individualised pricing.
whyItMatters: The machinery exists, and the open question is how much it is used.

title: Instacart showed shoppers different prices for the same groceries
hook: Same store, same time, same item: up to five different prices.
collected: Which test group a shopper was assigned to (Instacart says not personal or demographic data).
howObtained: Instacart's Eversight pricing tool ran price experiments for some retailers.
inferred: How demand changes at different prices (a price test).
done: Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative and More Perfect Union had 437 volunteers shop the same items at the same time (193 submissions analysed). About 74% of items appeared at more than one price; the average gap between lowest and highest was 13%, up to 23%.
affected: Shoppers at participating retailers on Instacart.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Investigation REPORTED by Consumer Reports and partners; Instacart confirmed the tests existed (company admission). There is no evidence they used personal data.

companyResponse.text: Instacart said the tests were randomised and "never" used personal, demographic or user-level behavioural data, and later ended them: "if two families are shopping for the same items, at the same time, from the same store location on Instacart, they see the same prices — period."

outcome.text: Instacart ended item price tests in December 2025. Reuters reported an FTC civil investigative demand. (A separate $60 million FTC settlement about delivery fees is a different case.)

sources.title: Instacart price investigation
Instacart ends AI price test after Consumer Reports investigation

limits: Random price testing is not personalised pricing. It still means two neighbours can pay different amounts.
whyItMatters: Shows that a price can be an experiment you never agreed to join.

title: Viral claims of an 'iPhone tax' on quick-commerce apps
hook: Screenshots showed grapes at ₹65 on Android and ₹146 on an iPhone.
collected: Device type, which any app knows.
inferred: Claimed: iPhone users will pay more.
done: Users posted side-by-side screenshots of Zepto showing different prices on Android and iPhone. India's consumer affairs minister directed the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) to look into such complaints.
label: ALLEGED
labelNote: Viral screenshots; no controlled test. Other users suggested a 'Super Saver' mode explained the gap.

companyResponse.text: Zepto did not respond to afaqs' request for comment. We found no published response.

sources.title: Influencers expose price bias as q-comm platforms levy 'Apple tax'

limits: Two screenshots cannot rule out other differences (location, account, offers, time). See the Auditor's Lab.
whyItMatters: The claim may or may not be true, and the way to settle it is a fair test.

title: Amazon Prime sign-up and cancellation: $2.5 billion
hook: The button said 'No, I don't want Free Shipping'. Cancelling had its own internal code name.
inferred: Who could be nudged into a subscription.
done: The FTC alleged Amazon enrolled consumers in Prime without consent through confusing checkout designs and made cancelling hard through a multi-step process internally called 'Iliad'.
affected: About 35 million consumers, per the FTC.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Court-approved settlement. Amazon did not admit wrongdoing.

companyResponse.text: "Amazon and our executives have always followed the law, and this settlement allows us to move forward and focus on innovating for customers."
companyResponse.source: Amazon spokesperson Mark Blafkin, via press coverage

outcome.text: $1 billion civil penalty plus $1.5 billion in refunds. It requires a clear decline button, clear terms, and cancellation as easy as sign-up.

sources.title: FTC Secures Historic $2.5 Billion Settlement Against Amazon
Amazon to pay $2.5 billion to settle FTC allegations

limits: Settled during trial, so the allegations were not decided by a court.
whyItMatters: The largest FTC dark-patterns penalty to date, and the designs it describes are ones you have probably clicked.

title: Epic Games: Fortnite purchase design and children's privacy ($520 million)
hook: One button press could buy something; voice chat with strangers was on by default for kids.
collected: Children's personal information; in-game purchase behaviour.
inferred: Not the core issue. The case was about design and consent.
done: The FTC alleged Epic used dark patterns that led players into unwanted purchases, locked accounts of people who disputed charges, and broke children's privacy law, including turning voice and text chat on by default.
affected: Fortnite players, many of them children.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC orders. Epic did not admit wrongdoing.

companyResponse.text: Epic wrote that "no developer creates a game with the intention of ending up here" and said the laws had not changed but their application had.

outcome.text: $275 million penalty under the children's privacy law (COPPA) plus $245 million in refunds: $520 million total.

sources.title: Fortnite Video Game Maker Epic Games to Pay More Than Half a Billion Dollars
Epic Games agrees to pay record-breaking $520 million

whyItMatters: Game design choices can be consumer-protection issues.

title: FTC v. Uber: the Uber One subscription
hook: Up to 23 screens and 32 actions to cancel, the FTC claims.
done: The FTC alleges Uber enrolled people in Uber One without consent, overstated its savings, and made cancellation take up to 23 screens and 32 actions.
label: ALLEGED

companyResponse.text: Uber said it was disappointed and that cancelling takes about 20 seconds in the app.

sources.title: FTC Takes Action Against Uber for Deceptive Billing and Cancellation Practices

whyItMatters: The same 'roach motel' pattern (easy to enter, hard to leave) as the Amazon case.

title: FTC and states v. Live Nation/Ticketmaster: hidden fees
hook: The advertised ticket price was lower than what you really paid, the FTC says.
done: The FTC and seven states allege Ticketmaster advertised prices lower than the total, revealing fees (in some cases up to 44%) late in checkout, and misrepresented ticket limits.
label: ALLEGED
labelNote: Lawsuit filed; not decided. A separate DC drip-pricing settlement ($9.9 million, April 2026) was reported.

companyResponse.text: Ticketmaster said it now uses all-in pricing consistent with FTC rules and denied engaging in unfair or deceptive acts; Live Nation has moved to dismiss parts of the case, arguing the FTC misreads the 2016 BOTS Act.
companyResponse.source: Company statements and filings, via secondary coverage (Relix, Hypebot)

sources.title: FTC sues Live Nation and Ticketmaster
Live Nation and Ticketmaster File to Dismiss FTC Ticket Resale Lawsuit

whyItMatters: Drip pricing is one of India's 13 named dark patterns too.

title: Dark patterns at scale: a crawl of 11,000 shopping sites
hook: Fake countdowns and 'only 2 left' messages, found by a robot that shopped 53,000 product pages.
collected: Not applicable (a measurement of website designs).
done: Mathur et al. (ACM CSCW 2019) crawled about 53,000 product pages on about 11,000 shopping sites and found 1,818 dark-pattern instances of 15 types. 183 websites used clearly deceptive practices, and 22 third-party companies sold dark patterns as ready-made services.
label: DOCUMENTED

sources.title: Dark Patterns at Scale: Findings from a Crawl of 11K Shopping Websites

limits: A lower bound: the crawler could not see every pattern.
whyItMatters: Some 'urgency' messages are fake, and some are sold as plug-ins.

title: The FTC's 'Click-to-Cancel' rule was struck down
hook: A rule to make cancelling as easy as signing up was vacated days before it took effect.
done: The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the FTC's rule on procedural grounds (missing preliminary regulatory analysis) on 8 July 2025, before its 14 July compliance date.
label: DOCUMENTED

outcome.text: Rule vacated; state auto-renewal laws still apply.

sources.title: Eighth Circuit vacates FTC Click-to-Cancel rule

limits: Procedural ruling, not a ruling that the practices are fine.
whyItMatters: Protections can disappear; enforcement is uneven.

title: India names 13 dark patterns in official guidelines
hook: India's consumer regulator listed false urgency, basket sneaking, confirm-shaming and ten more.
done: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) issued the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023, under the Consumer Protection Act 2019. The 13 patterns: false urgency, basket sneaking, confirm shaming, forced action, subscription trap, interface interference, bait and switch, drip pricing, disguised advertisement, nagging, trick question, SaaS billing, and rogue malware.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Official government guidelines. A June 2025 advisory asking platforms to self-audit is reported by secondary sources.

outcome.text: In force; enforcement so far is mainly notices (for example on 'advance tips').

sources.title: Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023

limits: We could not open the official government PDF (blocked). No separate penalty is specified in the guidelines.
whyItMatters: A clear list helps ordinary users name what they see.

title: 52 of 53 top Indian apps used deceptive design
hook: An industry study counted 2.7 dark patterns per app on average.
howObtained: Review of more than 12,000 app screens.
done: ASCI Academy and design firm Parallel HQ reviewed 53 popular Indian apps across 9 industries and found deceptive patterns in 52, averaging 2.7 per app; health-tech apps were highest.
label: REPORTED
labelNote: Industry self-regulatory body's study with a described method; not a regulator finding. Apps were not all named publicly.

sources.title: 52 of 53 top apps in India use dark patterns, says ASCI study

limits: We could not read the report PDF directly.
whyItMatters: Dark patterns are the norm, not the exception.

title: Rite Aid's facial recognition falsely flagged shoppers
hook: Cameras matched shoppers to a watchlist, and many matches were wrong.
inferred: Whether a shopper matched a 'person of interest' (suspected shoplifter).
done: The FTC alleged the system produced thousands of false matches, falling more heavily on women and people of colour, who could then be followed, searched or asked to leave.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC order. Rite Aid disagreed with the allegations.

companyResponse.text: Rite Aid said it "fundamentally disagree[s]" with the allegations and that the technology was a limited pilot it had stopped more than three years earlier.
companyResponse.source: Rite Aid statement via press coverage

outcome.text: Five-year ban on using facial recognition for surveillance.

sources.title: FTC bans Rite Aid from using facial surveillance systems for five years

limits: We could not open the FTC's own page.
whyItMatters: Automated suspicion can treat innocent people as suspects, unequally.
